title: Enhancing achievement and retention in circle geometry through digital storytelling for senior secondary learners
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether digital storytelling can improve senior secondary students’ achievement and retention in circle geometry, and whether effects differ by gender. The authors note persistent difficulties in mathematics learning, especially in abstract topics like geometry, and argue that digital storytelling may make concepts more engaging and easier to understand by combining narrative with multimedia elements.

The study used a pretest-posttest non-equivalent control group quasi-experimental design with 132 Senior Secondary School One students from four public schools in Nsukka Local Government Area, Enugu State, Nigeria. The experimental group was taught circle geometry through digital storytelling activities using tools such as Canva, Sway, GeoGebra, and Kahoot!, while the control group received conventional lecture-based instruction. Students completed a Geometry Achievement Test before instruction, after instruction, and again four weeks later for retention.

Results showed that students taught with digital storytelling outperformed those taught conventionally on both achievement and retention outcomes. The paper also found no significant gender differences and no significant interaction between instructional method and gender. The authors conclude that digital storytelling is an effective approach for teaching circle geometry in secondary mathematics classrooms and recommend its use by mathematics teachers.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest non-equivalent control group study with ANCOVA, a reasonable design for classroom intervention research but without random assignment. Internal validity is strengthened by pretesting, covariate adjustment, and reported reliability (KR-20=0.83), though selection bias remains a concern.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported achievement effect is very large (ηp²=0.843) and retention effect is also substantial (ηp²=0.380), indicating strong positive impact in a priority K-12 mathematics population. Even allowing for quasi-experimental limitations, the magnitude suggests meaningful educational benefit.

interventions.use_case: digital storytelling-supported mathematics instruction for senior secondary circle geometry, combining narrated multimedia stories, GeoGebra exploration, Kahoot quizzes, and student-created story presentations

finding.finding_summary: Digital storytelling produced substantially higher circle geometry achievement than conventional instruction for senior secondary learners (n=132). The experimental group’s posttest mean rose from 62.31 (SD=7.31) to 93.37 (SD=5.87), while the control group rose from 61.73 (SD=6.82) to 64.70 (SD=6.85); ANCOVA showed a significant group effect, F(1,127)=681.008, p<.05, ηp²=0.843.
finding.measure: Geometry Achievement Test (GAT) posttest scores on circle geometry
finding.std_deviation: experimental post SD=5.87; control post SD=6.85

finding.finding_summary: Retention in circle geometry was significantly higher for the digital storytelling group than for the conventional group. The paper reports a retention mean of 95.97 (SD=3.67) for the experimental group versus 64.08 (SD=6.73) for the control group, with ANCOVA indicating a significant group difference, F(1,127)=77.976, p<.05, ηp²=0.380.
finding.measure: Retention test scores on circle geometry four weeks after posttest
finding.std_deviation: experimental retention SD=3.67; control retention SD=6.73

finding.finding_summary: The study found no significant gender differences in achievement within the digital storytelling condition, suggesting the intervention benefited male and female learners similarly on performance outcomes. Gender was non-significant in ANCOVA, F(1,127)=0.113, p=.738, ηp²=0.001.
finding.measure: Achievement scores by gender on the GAT
finding.study_size: n=68 in digital storytelling group for gender comparison

finding.finding_summary: Gender did not significantly affect retention outcomes under digital storytelling, indicating no evidence of differential persistence of learning for male versus female learners. The paper reports a non-significant gender effect for retention in ANCOVA, though the exact F-statistic is not shown in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Retention scores by gender after digital storytelling instruction
finding.study_size: n=68 in digital storytelling group for gender comparison

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports no significant interaction between instructional method and gender on achievement, indicating the digital storytelling benefit was broadly similar across boys and girls. The interaction effect was small and non-significant, F(1,127)=1.127, p=.290, ηp²=0.009.
finding.measure: Interaction effect on achievement in circle geometry
